Gold & Treasury Yields — Cointegration Testing

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

What is Cointegration?

Two I(1) series are said to be cointegrated if a linear combination of them is stationary. Intuitively, even though each series wanders randomly on its own, they move together in the long run — they share a common stochastic trend.

In our case, cointegration between gold and the 10Y yield would mean that deviations from the long-run equilibrium relationship are temporary and self-correcting — which is precisely what H1 and H2 require.

The Johansen Test

The Johansen test is the standard multivariate framework for cointegration. It tests for the number of cointegrating vectors \(r\) in a system of I(1) series.

We test sequentially:

\[H_0: r = 0 \quad \text{(no cointegration)}\] \[H_0: r \leq 1 \quad \text{(at most one cointegrating vector)}\]

Rejecting \(r = 0\) and failing to reject \(r \leq 1\) confirms exactly one cointegrating relationship — which is what we expect in a bivariate system.

The test comes in two variants:

  • Trace test : tests whether the number of cointegrating vectors is less than \(r\)
  • Maximum eigenvalue test : tests whether there are exactly \(r\) cointegrating vectors

We report both.

Setup

Code 
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(urca)

panel <- read_parquet("../data/macro_panel.parquet")

# Bind series into a matrix — required by ca.jo()
y <- cbind(panel$gold, panel$yield)
colnames(y) <- c("gold", "yield")

Lag Selection

The Johansen test requires specifying the number of lags. We use the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to select the optimal lag length.

Code 
library(vars) 

lag_select <- VARselect(y, lag.max = 10, type = "const")
optimal_lag <- lag_select$selection["AIC(n)"]

cat("Optimal lag (AIC):", optimal_lag, "\n")
Optimal lag (AIC): 5

Johansen Test — Trace

Code 
joh_trace <- ca.jo(
  y,
  type  = "trace",
  ecdet = "const",
  K     = optimal_lag
)

summary(joh_trace)

###################### 
# Johansen-Procedure # 
###################### 

Test type: trace statistic , without linear trend and constant in cointegration 

Eigenvalues (lambda):
[1]  2.904754e-03  1.192352e-03 -4.336809e-19

Values of teststatistic and critical values of test:

          test 10pct  5pct  1pct
r <= 1 |  4.42  7.52  9.24 12.97
r = 0  | 15.19 17.85 19.96 24.60

Eigenvectors, normalised to first column:
(These are the cointegration relations)

            gold.l5  yield.l5  constant
gold.l5      1.0000    1.0000     1.000
yield.l5   747.3142 -828.2435   255.721
constant -2577.1757  462.0153 -3553.071

Weights W:
(This is the loading matrix)

             gold.l5      yield.l5      constant
gold.d  7.949727e-04 -3.841334e-04  1.341517e-18
yield.d 2.741204e-07  2.314914e-06 -2.544836e-21

Johansen Test — Maximum Eigenvalue

Code 
joh_eigen <- ca.jo(
  y,
  type  = "eigen",
  ecdet = "const",
  K     = optimal_lag
)

summary(joh_eigen)

###################### 
# Johansen-Procedure # 
###################### 

Test type: maximal eigenvalue statistic (lambda max) , without linear trend and constant in cointegration 

Eigenvalues (lambda):
[1]  2.904754e-03  1.192352e-03 -4.336809e-19

Values of teststatistic and critical values of test:

          test 10pct  5pct  1pct
r <= 1 |  4.42  7.52  9.24 12.97
r = 0  | 10.77 13.75 15.67 20.20

Eigenvectors, normalised to first column:
(These are the cointegration relations)

            gold.l5  yield.l5  constant
gold.l5      1.0000    1.0000     1.000
yield.l5   747.3142 -828.2435   255.721
constant -2577.1757  462.0153 -3553.071

Weights W:
(This is the loading matrix)

             gold.l5      yield.l5      constant
gold.d  7.949727e-04 -3.841334e-04  1.341517e-18
yield.d 2.741204e-07  2.314914e-06 -2.544836e-21

Interpretation

For each test, we compare the test statistic to the critical value at 5%:

  • For the Trace test, for \(H_0: r = 0\) , the test-statistic is of 17.39, which is below the critical value at 5% (19.96) and even below the critical value at 10% (17.85).
  • For the Eigenvalue test, also for \(H_0: r = 0\) , the test-statistic is of 13.24, which is also below the critical values at 5% (15.67) and at 10% (13.75).

We expected this first H0 to be rejected, but in both cases we fail to reject it.

Conclusion

The cointegration test has failed on the full time window. Still, by looking at the descriptive statistics, we see graphical evidences of a potential inflexion point around 2022 in the relationship of the two curves. We will therefore re-investigate the cointegration between 2011 and 2022.

## What is Cointegration?

Two I(1) series are said to be **cointegrated** if a linear combination of them is stationary. Intuitively, even though each series wanders randomly on its own, they move together in the long run — they share a common stochastic trend.

In our case, cointegration between gold and the 10Y yield would mean that deviations from the long-run equilibrium relationship are temporary and self-correcting — which is precisely what H1 and H2 require.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The Johansen Test

The **Johansen test** is the standard multivariate framework for cointegration. It tests for the number of cointegrating vectors $r$ in a system of I(1) series.

We test sequentially:

$$H_0: r = 0 \quad \text{(no cointegration)}$$ $$H_0: r \leq 1 \quad \text{(at most one cointegrating vector)}$$

Rejecting $r = 0$ and failing to reject $r \leq 1$ confirms exactly one cointegrating relationship — which is what we expect in a bivariate system.

The test comes in two variants:

-   **Trace test** : tests whether the number of cointegrating vectors is less than $r$
-   **Maximum eigenvalue test** : tests whether there are exactly $r$ cointegrating vectors

We report both.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Setup

```{r}
library(arrow)
library(tidyverse)
library(urca)

panel <- read_parquet("../data/macro_panel.parquet")

# Bind series into a matrix — required by ca.jo()
y <- cbind(panel$gold, panel$yield)
colnames(y) <- c("gold", "yield")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Lag Selection

The Johansen test requires specifying the number of lags. We use the **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)** to select the optimal lag length.

```{r}
library(vars) 

lag_select <- VARselect(y, lag.max = 10, type = "const")
optimal_lag <- lag_select$selection["AIC(n)"]

cat("Optimal lag (AIC):", optimal_lag, "\n")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Johansen Test — Trace

```{r}
joh_trace <- ca.jo(
  y,
  type  = "trace",
  ecdet = "const",
  K     = optimal_lag
)

summary(joh_trace)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Johansen Test — Maximum Eigenvalue

```{r}
joh_eigen <- ca.jo(
  y,
  type  = "eigen",
  ecdet = "const",
  K     = optimal_lag
)

summary(joh_eigen)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Interpretation

For each test, we compare the **test statistic** to the **critical value at 5%**:

-   For the Trace test, for $H_0: r = 0$ , the test-statistic is of 17.39, which is below the critical value at 5% (19.96) and even below the critical value at 10% (17.85).
-   For the Eigenvalue test, also for $H_0: r = 0$ , the test-statistic is of 13.24, which is also below the critical values at 5% (15.67) and at 10% (13.75).

**We** **expected this first H0 to be rejected**, but in both cases we fail to reject it.

## Conclusion

The cointegration test has failed on the full time window. Still, by looking at the descriptive statistics, we see graphical evidences of a potential inflexion point around 2022 in the relationship of the two curves. We will therefore re-investigate the cointegration between 2011 and 2022.
